title: I believe, we believe (CCC 166–167)
hook: faith is personal but never solitary

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four senses of scripture: literal, allegorical, moral, anagogical. Your line was one text, four depths. Which line opened a second layer? Today, the first words of the Creed. Day one thousand sixty-seven.

A Sunday afternoon baptism. The baby is asleep, or furious. The priest turns to the parents and godparents and asks them, one question at a time, whether they believe in God, the Father almighty, and in his Son, and in the Holy Spirit. And each time they answer out loud: I do. Then, the next Sunday morning, at an ordinary Mass, the whole church stands and says the Creed together, every voice at once. Same faith. One time it sounds like a single voice; the next, like a crowd. Today: I believe, we believe.
screen: `A BAPTISM: I DO.` → `A SUNDAY MASS: EVERY VOICE AT ONCE.` → `I BELIEVE, WE BELIEVE.`

segments.voice: The Catechism notices the grammar. It says I believe is the faith of the Church professed by each believer personally, above all at baptism; that's how the Apostles' Creed speaks. And we believe is the faith confessed by the bishops gathered in council, or by the whole assembly at worship; that's how the creed of the councils speaks. Both are true at once. Faith, the Catechism says, is a personal act: a person's free response to God who reveals himself. But faith is never an isolated act either. And then comes the line behind today's carry. No one can believe alone, the Catechism says, just as no one can live alone. Nobody gave themselves faith, any more than they gave themselves life. It was received from others, and it's meant to be handed on. There's a moment in Mark's Gospel that holds both sides. A father brings his son, who is suffering terribly, to Jesus. Jesus speaks of believing, and the father cries out, in the Douay-Rheims, "I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief." It's as personal as a sentence can be. And he says it in a crowd, on someone else's behalf, for his child. The Catechism recalls the baptism rite of the Roman Ritual, where the minister asks what is being sought from God's Church, and the answer is one word: faith. The Church, it says, believes first, and carries each believer. That's the carry: no one believes alone. Even a private prayer, in the Catholic picture, is said inside a very large we.
screen: `I BELIEVE: EACH ONE, AT BAPTISM.` · `WE BELIEVE: THE CHURCH TOGETHER.` · `NO ONE BELIEVES ALONE.` · `I DO BELIEVE; HELP MY UNBELIEF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say the Creed with others. If you can, say it with someone, at Mass, at home, or quietly along with a recording. If you're on your own right now, try this. Settle, and breathe. Say the first two words, I believe, or just think them. Then let faces come to mind: the people whose faith reached you somehow, a grandparent, a teacher, a friend, a stranger in a pew. Hold them for a moment. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. If you don't, think of who carried what you know, in any part of life. The bell holds the time.
I believe. The first words of the Creed: personal, said by each one, and never said alone. Today's word.
Your line: no one believes alone. Today, catch one thing you believe, about God or about anything, and name who first handed it to you. Day one thousand sixty-seven.

howItsDone: At baptism, the parents and godparents of a child, or the adult being baptized, profess the faith by answering the priest's questions; at Sunday Mass the congregation stands and says the Creed together.

fork.setup: in the Roman Ritual's baptism rite the Catechism recalls, the minister asks what is being sought from God's Church. what's the answer?
fork.reveal: faith. the Catechism uses the question to show that faith is received from the Church before anyone says I believe on their own.

original.note: Latin: I believe. The first word of the Apostles' Creed in Latin.

trapdoor: what you thought: faith is a private thing, just between one person and God.
what it means: faith is a personal act, but received from others and held together: I believe, inside we believe.
what a scholar hears: CCC 166–167: 'I believe' of the baptismal creed, 'we believe' of the councils; no one can believe alone, just as no one can live alone.

notes: Confirm Challoner wording of Mark 9:23 (Mark 9:24 in most modern Bibles).

Catechism paraphrased (copyright): CCC 166 (personal act, not isolated; no one can believe alone as no one can live alone; faith received and handed on), CCC 167 ('I believe' and 'we believe'), CCC 168 (the Church believes first; the baptismal question and answer 'faith'). Confirm.

Hook: baptismal questions paraphrased loosely (renunciations omitted); in the current rite the parents' answer to 'what do you ask of God's Church' is usually 'baptism'; the fork therefore says 'the old baptismal rite the Catechism recalls'. Confirm.
Original: Latin 'Credo'; the note says it's why it's called a creed. That is an etymology claim not stated in CCC 166–167; Note now says only that it opens the Latin Apostles' Creed.
Practice adapted from the outline's 'pray the Creed with others' to 'say the Creed with others' so anyone can join.

Editor: cut 'nobody can make that response for you', which the CCC does not say and which clashes with the hook's infant baptism; 'an old baptismal rite' corrected to the Roman Ritual, as CCC 168 names it (teach and fork).
